clue.text: The hours oddly spent churning over and over secret

indicators.note: churned letters are stirred into a new order
the odd letters of THE HOURS are used up, so only the even ones stay

parts.note: tHe hOuRs: the even letters, once the odd ones are spent
the churned HHUS, HUSH, said twice over

explanation.surface: Someone frittering away the night, going over and over a secret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over and over' doubles the word, the way the answer itself says HUSH twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Hush-hush is an informal doubled word for secret, built from 'hush' as a call for silence.

clue.text: What about launching a Soviet climber?

indicators.note: in a down clue, launching sends A RED upwards, so it reads bottom to top

explanation.surface: A question about a Soviet mountaineer, or a Soviet space launch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' suggests a mountaineer or cosmonaut; here it is a climbing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Hedera is the ivy genus, a classic climbing plant.

clue.text: Standards slipping, we fly at night

definitions.note: a clause spoken by the answer: sand-darts are moths

indicators.note: slipping standards lose their order

explanation.surface: A night-flying pilot or a nocturnal creature complaining that standards are slipping.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer speaks in the first person: 'we' are the moths themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: The sand-dart is a noctuid moth, and moths fly at night.

clue.text: See Phoebe, Bull and edges of 7 flying in astronomical equipment

indicators.note: letters sent flying land in a new order
the edges of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: 7 is COMET; its edges are C and T

explanation.surface: An invitation to view Phoebe (a moon of Saturn), Taurus the Bull and a comet through a telescope.
explanation.walkthrough: '7' refers to the answer at 7 down, COMET.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hubble Space Telescope is a piece of astronomical equipment in orbit.

clue.text: Discussion group remains animated

indicators.note: animated letters are set moving into a new order

explanation.surface: A discussion group that stays lively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remains' reads as a verb (stays) but is simply the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a seminar is a class where a small group talks a topic through with a tutor.

clue.text: Stokes derides shifts

parts.note: S is a symbol for the stokes, the unit of kinematic viscosity

explanation.surface: Someone called Stokes sneering at changes of plan.
explanation.walkthrough: Stokes looks like a surname but is the physics unit, abbreviated S; 'shifts' are loose dresses, not changes.
explanation.definitionFit: A smock and a shift are both loose, simple dresses.

clue.text: People on radio to instruct landing outside Belgium are sadly cracking up

definitions.note: a verb phrase for a noun: cracking up is having one

parts.note: air traffic control talks a pilot down, instructing the landing by radio

indicators.note: 'sadly' treats ARE as going wrong, its letters out of place

parts.note: B is Belgium's international vehicle code

explanation.surface: Radio operators talking a craft down near Belgium, sadly falling apart.
explanation.walkthrough: Talk down is air traffic control jargon for guiding a pilot in by radio; B is Belgium's international vehicle code.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracking up is the informal idiom for suffering a collapse of the mind.

clue.text: I circle the sun bed occupied by mining engineer

definitions.note: a clause spoken by the answer, standing for a noun

indicators.note: a bed occupied by someone has them inside it

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
ME = mining engineer, the initials of the professional title

explanation.surface: A mining engineer in a sunbed, circling the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun bed' tempts you to read a tanning bed; the sun belongs to the definition and the bed is a cot.
explanation.definitionFit: A comet orbits the sun, so it can say 'I circle the sun'.

clue.text: Most assuredly ground-to-air ceasefires will include confines of space

indicators.note: in a down clue, going from the ground up into the air turns the letters to read upwards

parts.note: the first and last letters of SpacE

explanation.surface: Missile ceasefires that extend to space make things most secure.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'ground-to-air' means reading upwards; the insertion happens first, then the whole thing flips.
explanation.definitionFit: Assuredly means securely, so the superlative 'most assuredly' is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Having visited e.g. 10, astronaut's back home at last, he says

definitions.note: a clause for a noun: a stater is one who states

parts.note: 10 across, DENEB, is an example of a star

indicators.note: a word's back is its final letter
'at last' means at the very end, so only the final letter of home is taken

explanation.surface: An astronaut home after visiting a distant star, telling his story.
explanation.walkthrough: The T and E are the ones that went visiting, so they end up inside STAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A stater is someone who states, so 'he says' describes him.

clue.text: Vertex of Summer Triangle — dependably evident nightly — essentially blue at the outset

indicators.note: each word's outset is its first letter

explanation.surface: A bright star, reliably seen every night, with a bluish look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essentially' looks like a middle-letters signal, but it is one of the five words whose first letters spell the star.
explanation.definitionFit: Deneb, in Cygnus, is one of the three corners of the Summer Triangle, with Vega and Altair.

clue.text: Scintillating 7, in my flying visits, representative of the bigger picture

indicators.note: a scintillating comet flickers, its letters dancing
IN MY sent flying lands in a new order

explanation.surface: A sparkling comet paying flying visits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scintillating' and 'flying' each signal an anagram of their own word group, so there are two scrambles, not one.
explanation.definitionFit: In metonymy one associated thing stands for a larger whole, as 'the Crown' for the monarchy.

clue.text: New lander first to penetrate alien world

indicators.note: a new LANDER is a remade one, its letters rearranged
the first letter of penetrate

explanation.surface: A new space lander making the first descent into an alien world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alien world' reads as one phrase, but ALIEN is ET and 'world' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Mars, nicknamed for its rusty colour, is one world among many.

clue.text: Ara represents this single missing blue-green star

indicators.note: ALTAIR missing its single I

parts.note: ALTAIR, the star, with its I removed

explanation.surface: A note on a constellation and a star of unusual colour.
explanation.walkthrough: Ara is a southern constellation whose name is Latin for altar.
explanation.definitionFit: Ara is Latin for the thing it names, and the constellation's figure is drawn as one, so it represents it.

clue.text: Evidence of fall, meteoric for one boxer

definitions.text: Evidence of fall, meteoric for one
definitions.meaning: the hollow a falling meteorite leaves, a meteoric one being one example
one who crates things, packing them in boxes

explanation.surface: A boxer whose fall was spectacular, meteoric even.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxer' is not a fighter but someone who puts things in crates.
explanation.definitionFit: A meteorite's fall leaves a crater; a crater is also one who crates, boxing things up.

clue.text: Returning carrier ship receiving earth pictures, not immediately decipherable?

parts.note: Uber, the ride-hailing company, carries passengers

explanation.surface: An aircraft carrier coming home with photographs of Earth that need analysing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrier ship' reads as one warship, but they are two parts: the taxi firm and SS.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebus is a picture puzzle standing for words, so it is not immediately decipherable.

clue.text: It takes a lot to learn

definitions.text: It takes a lot to learn

parts.note: the surface reads 'it needs a great deal'; the setter means it carries a large number of passengers
not the effort of study but the destination: taking children to where they learn

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as 'learning is hard work', but it takes a lot of children to where they learn.
explanation.definitionFit: A school bus carries a busload of pupils to school.

clue.text: Characteristic of fans not winning game

indicators.note: 'not winning' asks for the fans' word with the sense of winning taken out, so those letters go

parts.note: SUPPORTIVE, like fans, with UP taken out

explanation.surface: Fans loyal to a team even when it is losing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like a match but is the adjective: up for fun.
explanation.definitionFit: Game and sportive both mean playful, willing for fun.

clue.text: Pounds, shillings and pence, steel warped

definitions.note: a verb for a plural noun: pestles are the things that pound

indicators.note: warped letters are bent out of order

explanation.surface: Old British money, pounds, shillings and pence, and some bent steel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pounds' sits in the list as money, but it is the definition: things that pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Pestles pound things in a mortar.

clue.text: Group aboard last couple of rockets set up midnight rendezvous

indicators.note: in a down clue, setting up turns the letters to read upwards
the last two letters of rockets

explanation.surface: A band boarding a rocket, set up for a midnight launch.
explanation.walkthrough: ABBA goes between the T and S, and T(ABBA)S then reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore witches meet at midnight for this assembly, so it is a rendezvous by definition of its hour.

clue.text: One helps out leading characters

indicators.note: HELPS out of order, rearranged

explanation.surface: A helper supporting the lead actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading characters' reads as stars of a show; here they are letters that lead an alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, the leading character.

clue.text: University types created cycles in unit

definitions.note: a plural noun for a collective noun: academe is the academic world and its people

parts.note: an ace is a one, a unit

explanation.surface: Academics inventing bicycles or cycles of research.
explanation.walkthrough: In cycling the letters keep their order but rotate: M goes from front to back.
explanation.definitionFit: Academe is the world of universities and the people in it.

clue.text: Hardly the sphere of the old-fashioned scientist!

parts.note: gives no letters: it flips 'old-fashioned' to its opposite
'hardly' old-fashioned points to the opposite, a word for modern
the ton was the old word for fashionable society, the sphere of the fashionable

explanation.surface: A joke that an old-fashioned scientist would hardly be at home in modern circles.
explanation.walkthrough: The ton means fashionable society; a new ton is the last place for the old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Newton is the most famous of scientists.

clue.text: Sample from traveller in G-suit, features of Saturn

indicators.note: a sample is a small piece taken from the words that follow

explanation.surface: Samples brought back by a space traveller in a G-suit, from Saturn.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in G-suit is ignored, so the letters run straight on.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturn's rings are its best-known feature.

clue.text: Stars suddenly brighter and twinkly on average, before storm

indicators.note: twinkling letters flicker into a new order

parts.note: ON AVERAGE up to the RAGE

explanation.surface: Stars that brighten suddenly and twinkle averagely before a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: AVERAGE ends in RAGE, so the part before the storm is ON AVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Novae are stars that flare suddenly to many times their brightness.

clue.text: Buzz's first problem after shortage — result of huge collapse

indicators.note: 'after' places the problem later in the line than the shortage
Buzz's first is what comes first in Buzz, its opening letter

parts.note: to be in a hole is to be in trouble

explanation.surface: Buzz Aldrin's first problem being a shortage on a mission.
explanation.walkthrough: Buzz calls up Aldrin, the astronaut, but only its B is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A black hole forms when a huge star collapses under its own gravity.

clue.text: One new member of quartet, Tim Peake, gutted Virgin

parts.note: a string quartet has a viola

indicators.note: a gutted name loses its insides, keeping its outer letters

parts.note: Tim Peake is a British astronaut; his outer letters are T and E

explanation.surface: A new crew member joins Tim Peake on a Virgin space flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Virgin' looks like the space company but is the definition; 'quartet' means a string quartet, not a crew.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgin as an adjective means never touched or violated, a plain synonym.

clue.text: As an alternative, cut celestial path

parts.note: a cut is a share, a bit

explanation.surface: An option to shorten the route a spacecraft takes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' reads as a verb but is a noun, a portion.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbit is the path a body takes through space.

clue.text: Cherished by SpaceX — Eternal City

indicators.note: the answer is held close by the words around it

explanation.surface: SpaceX's affection for Rome, the Eternal City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eternal City' is Rome, but the phrase is split: ETERNAL helps hide the answer and 'City' alone defines it. Exeter is a cathedral city in Devon.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the county town of Devon, in south-west England, is a cathedral city.

clue.text: Linesman's not one for stress plugging in Empire State

indicators.note: 'not one' asks for the stress word without its I, so that letter goes

parts.note: New York is the Empire State

explanation.surface: A football linesman stressed out in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Linesman' is not a football official but a writer of lines of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was a poet, a writer of lines.
